title.en: The Self Alone: Prajapati Creates and Divides (Brihadaranyaka 1.4)
title.zh: 唯我獨存：生主創世而自分（大森林奧義書）

region.zh: 韋提訶國彌提羅（遮那迦王廷，象徵性定位）

texts.period: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, c. 8th-6th c. BCE (Müller translation, 1884)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 15)
source.work: The Upanishads, Part II, trans. F. Max Müller (SBE 15, 1884), Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, Adhyaya I, Brahmana 4

summary.en: In the beginning the Self alone existed, in the form of a person. He looked around, saw nothing but himself, and said 'I am'. From fear, from loneliness, and from the desire for a second, he divided himself into man and wife, and from their union the world of beings, the gods, the elements and the castes proceed - death as hunger walks in from the very start, and the Self learns that to live is to give itself away.
summary.zh: 太初唯自我獨存，其形為人。彼環顧四周，所見唯己，乃言『我是』。由於恐懼、孤獨與欲得第二者，彼自分為夫妻，萬有、諸神、諸元素與種姓皆由其結合而出——死亡作為飢餓自始即行，而自我學會：活著即是將自己給出去。

sensitivity.note: Canonical sruti scripture; classified 'religious' rather than 'myth'.

passages.text: In the beginning this universe was Self alone, in the shape of a person. Looking round, he saw nothing else but himself; and his first words were 'I am'. Hence the name 'I' arose even now, for he who is called the Self first said so.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.4.1-2 (Müller 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: He feared, and therefore people fear being alone; then he thought: as there is nothing else but myself, what should I fear? - and his fear left him, for what should he have feared? It is he alone who is beyond fear. Yet he was not happy, alone as one; he longed for a second person, and he was as large as a man and a woman in close embrace; he divided his body into two, and from that division arose husband and wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.4.3 (Müller 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: From their union human beings were born. The wife reflected: how can he unite with me whom he produced from himself? - well, let me hide; she became a cow, he a bull, and cattle were born; she a mare, he a stallion; she a she-ass, he a he-ass - one species after another was generated down to the ants. Then he stretched himself and wept: 'for what cause have I been born, if there is no one but myself?' - and his tears and sweat became the year and the rains.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.4.3-5 (Müller 1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: He was afraid of death, who is hunger; death thought: there is nothing for me to eat here but him - and the Self devised speech, breath, sight, hearing, mind and deeds as his offerings, and with milk, with rain, with the sevenfold offering he fed death and made him part of the order. Thus he learned that he would not be preserved unless he gave himself; the teaching closes: giving is the nature of the fullness of sacrifice - the Self, giving itself, becomes the world's food and the world's maker at once.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.4.6-11 (Müller 1884); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: F. Max Müller, The Upanishads, Part II (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 15), Oxford, 1884 (public domain); modern: Patrick Olivelle, The Early Upanisads, Oxford, 1998

narrative.en:
Brihadaranyaka 1.4 is the Upanishads' great internalized cosmogony: the Vedic sacrifice-creation of the Purusha Sukta reimagined as a drama inside one Self. Where the Rigveda sacrifices a cosmic body, the Upanishad has the Self act alone.

In the beginning, the Self (Atman) alone existed, 'in the shape of a person'. He looked around and saw nothing but himself, and his first word was 'I am' - the text notes wryly that even now, when someone is called by name, it is this first utterance that answers. Then three movements.

First, fear: he was afraid, and thus 'people fear being alone' - but seeing nothing else to fear, he understood that fear of the Self alone is groundless, and dropped it; the teaching is that fear comes only from duality. Second, loneliness: he was not happy, alone as one; he longed for a second, and - the text's most startling image - he was as large as a husband and wife in close embrace, and he divided his body into two, and man and wife arose.

Third, the generation of the world, which is also its comedy: the wife, produced from him, reflects that she cannot unite with the one from whom she was born - 'let me hide' - and the sexes scatter across species. She becomes a cow, he a bull, and cattle are born; mare and stallion, she-ass and he-ass, each species generated in flight and pursuit, down to the ants. The world's creatures are the Self's descendants multiplied by evasion. He then stretches himself, weeps - 'for what cause have I been born, if there is no one but myself?' - and his tears and sweat become the rains and the year.

Hunger and death: the Self fears death, 'who is hunger'; death thinks that there is nothing here to eat but him. The Self's answer is the origin of sacrifice: he creates speech, breath, sight, hearing, mind, and work - makes them his offerings - and with milk, with rain, with the sevenfold offering he feeds death, converting the eater into a participant in the order. The doctrine closes with a formula that will echo through the tradition: the Self cannot be preserved except by giving itself; giving is the nature of the fullness of sacrifice.

Function: this Brahmana converts ritual theology into psychology. Creation is not an event in the past but the Self's continuing activity; fear, desire and hunger are cosmogonic forces; and the sacrifice is internalized - breath and speech are the oblations. The text prepares the Upanishads' two birds, 'tat tvam asi', and the Vedantic doctrine that the Self precedes the gods (the later verses of 1.4: 'the gods are later than the Self; those who worship them go to them, as to a shadow'). It also grounds caste and cosmic orders (the following sections derive Brahmins, Kshatriyas and the deities from the same Self's acts) - an internalizing cosmogony that still keeps the social map.
narrative.zh: 大森林奧義書 1.4 為奧義書最偉大的內在化創世敘事：將原人歌的祭祀創世重新想像為一個自我之內的戲劇。太初自我（阿特曼）獨存，『其形為人』；彼環顧四周，所見唯己，第一句話是『我是』——經文戲言至今凡人被呼名，回應者仍是這第一聲。繼而三個運動。恐懼：彼畏懼，故『人畏獨處』——然見無可懼者，遂悟懼由二元生而棄之。孤獨：彼獨一而不樂，欲得第二者——經文最驚人的意象——彼之大如夫妻相擁，自分其身為二，夫妻乃生。第三，世界之生成亦其喜劇：由彼而生的妻子思忖不能與生己者交合——『讓我躲藏』——兩性遂遁入萬類：她化母牛、他化公牛而生牛群；牝馬與牡馬、母驢與公驢，每一物種皆於逃避與追逐中生成，直至螞蟻。世界眾生即自我之子嗣經由閃避而倍增。彼伸展己身而哭泣——『若無他者，我為何而生？』——其淚與汗化為雨與年。飢餓與死亡：彼懼死亡，死亡即飢餓；死亡思忖此處唯彼可食。自我之答即祭祀之源：彼創言語、氣息、視、聽、心、業，以其為祭品，以乳、以雨、以七重供養餵養死亡，使食者化為秩序之參與者。教義結語將迴響於整個傳統：自我唯有捨己方能保存；給予即祭祀圓滿之性。功能：此梵書將儀式神學轉為心理學——創世非過去之事而是自我之持續活動；恐懼、欲望、飢餓皆為創世之力；祭祀被內化——氣息與言語即祭品。此篇預備了奧義書的雙鳥、『汝即彼』與整個吠檀多『自我先於諸神』之教，同時仍保留社會圖譜（後續篇章自同一自我之行為派生婆羅門、剎帝利與諸神）。

functions: Internalized cosmogony: creation relocated into the Self - foundation of Vedantic psychology
Doctrine that fear, desire and hunger are cosmogonic forces
Origin of sacrifice as self-giving ('he cannot be preserved except by giving himself')
Derivation of castes and deities from one Self - social order read cosmologically

variants.name: Chandogya Upanishad's Sat-teaching (Uddalaka)
variants.summary: The same 'in the beginning' restated impersonally: Being alone, one without a second, sent forth fire and the elements - replacing the personified Self-dividing with a father's pedagogy ('tat tvam asi').

variants.name: Rigveda 10.90 (Purusha Sukta)
variants.summary: The older externalized counterpart: a cosmic body sacrificed and divided into world and castes; Brihadaranyaka keeps the division but moves it inside a single Self.

variants.name: Aitareya Upanishad's hunger-creation
variants.summary: The Self says 'let me create the worlds' and does so through hunger and speech - 'he who eats is the Self'; a shorter, more ritualized sibling of the same myth.

title.en: In the Beginning Was Being: Uddalaka Teaches Shvetaketu (Chandogya 6)
title.zh: 太初為「有」：鬱陀羅迦教授書陀葛多（歌者奧義書）

region.zh: 俱盧-般遮羅之地（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Chandogya Upanishad, c. 8th-6th c. BCE (Müller translation, 1879)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 1)
source.work: The Upanishads, Part I, trans. F. Max Müller (SBE 1, 1879), Chandogya Upanishad, Prapathaka VI

summary.en: A father questions his son, freshly returned from twelve years of Vedic study, and finds him conceited but unenlightened. Uddalaka then teaches creation: in the beginning was Being alone, one without a second, which willed 'may I be many' and sent forth fire, water, food - and entered each thing as its self, 'that thou art' (tat tvam asi), repeated through the chapter like a bell struck after every lesson.
summary.zh: 父親考問初從十二年吠陀求學歸來之子，發現其驕矜而未悟。鬱陀羅迦遂授創世之教：太初為『有』，一而無二；彼意念『願我為多』，乃生出火、水、食——並以自我入於每一物，『汝即彼』（tat tvam asi）一語如鐘聲，於每課之後反覆敲響。

passages.text: Shvetaketu, son of Uddalaka Aruni, was told by his father: live the student's life, for none of our family is a brahmin by neglect. At twelve he went away, studied all the Vedas for twelve years, and returned at twenty-four, proud, thinking himself learned. His father asked: did you ask for that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought thought, the unknown known? Shvetaketu admitted he had not.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chandogya Upanishad 6.1 (Müller 1879); not verbatim.

passages.text: The father answers with creation: in the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second. Some say that in the beginning this was Non-being - but how could Being arise from Non-being? Being alone, my dear, was this in the beginning. It thought: may I be many, may I grow forth - and it sent forth fire; fire willed and sent forth water; water willed and sent forth food. The elements came forth, each with the living self at its heart.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chandogya Upanishad 6.2 (Müller 1879); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the teaching through images, each sealed with the same sentence. As by one lump of clay everything made of clay is known - the variation is merely speech, a name - so the essence is clay. The bee gathers from many flowers and makes one honey; the rivers run to the sea and become the sea, which does not know 'this is that river'. The banyan seed cut open shows no tree inside; that subtle essence is the self of all things.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chandogya Upanishad 6.9-12 (Müller 1879); not verbatim.

passages.text: The father sets a final test: put this salt in water and come to me in the morning. The boy finds the salt gone, though the water remains; told to sip from the surface, the middle, the bottom, he tastes salt everywhere. The father says: in the same way, though thou dost not see Being in this body, it is indeed here - that subtle essence, in which all things have their self, is the Self; that thou art, Shvetaketu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Chandogya Upanishad 6.13 (Müller 1879); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: F. Max Müller, The Upanishads, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 1), Oxford, 1879 (public domain); modern: Patrick Olivelle, Upanisads, Oxford World's Classics, 1996

narrative.en:
Chandogya Upanishad 6 - the 'Uddalaka chapter' - is the oldest and most influential sustained creation-doctrine in Indian literature, told as a scene between a father and his son rather than as a hymn.

The frame is a family drama. Shvetaketu, at his father Uddalaka Aruni's instruction, goes off at twelve to live the student's life ('for none of our family is a brahmin by neglect'), studies the whole Veda for twelve years, and comes home at twenty-four 'proud, thinking himself learned'. The father's first question punctures him gently: did you ask for that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought thought, the unknown known? The son admits he has not. What follows is sixteen lessons, each ending with the same refrain - 'that thou art, Shvetaketu' (tat tvam asi) - repeated like a bell after every image.

The cosmology: 'In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second.' Uddalaka pauses to refute the rival view ('some say in the beginning was Non-being') with a logical jab - how could Being arise from Non-being? - and then proceeds: Being willed, 'may I be many, may I grow forth', and sent forth fire; fire sent forth water; water sent forth food. From these elements everything living is compounded, in graded proportions (the 'sixteen parts' doctrine): a hot thing is fire-dominant, a wet thing water-dominant, and so on. Being then entered into each thing, each with 'the living self at its heart', and became the name-and-form of the many - the self in every self. The teaching concludes with the striking verse: 'thou art the woman, thou art the man, thou art the youth and the maiden... thou art the old man leaning on his staff; thou art born facing every direction.'

The parables are the chapter's genius, each dissolving the boundary between parts and whole. The lump of clay: by knowing one lump, everything made of clay is known - 'the variation is merely speech, a name'. The bee's honey: gathered from many flowers, indistinguishable in essence. The rivers: running to the sea, they become the sea, which 'does not know, this is that river'. The banyan seed: split open, no tree inside - 'that subtle essence is the self of all'. And the salt: dissolved in water, invisible but tasted in every sip, from surface to bottom - 'though thou dost not see Being in this body, it is indeed here: that thou art'.

Function: this is the doctrine of sat ('Being') as the single substance of the cosmos, and of identity-in-difference between the individual and the absolute. Tat tvam asi becomes one of the four great mahavakyas of Vedanta; the pedagogical frame - a stubborn but sincere student, images that escalate from clay to salt - became the model for all later guru-transmission scenes. The refutation of Non-being marks the oldest surviving debate between being- and non-being-cosmogonies inside the tradition, in dialogue with the Nasadiya Sukta's open question.
narrative.zh: 歌者奧義書第六章——『鬱陀羅迦章』——為印度文獻中最古老且最具影響力的連貫創世教義，以父子對話之景而非頌歌呈現。框架為家庭戲劇：書陀葛多奉父命十二歲出外求學（『吾家不可無婆羅門之業』），十二年學畢全吠陀，二十四歲歸家，『自負，自以為有學』。父親首問溫和刺破：你曾求問那種『未聞者得聞、未思者得思、未知者得知』之教嗎？其子承認未嘗學之。隨後為十六課，每課同以一句結——『汝即彼，書陀葛多』（tat tvam asi）——如鐘聲於每個意象後敲響。宇宙論：『太初，吾兒，此為「有」，一而無二。』鬱陀羅迦先以邏輯反駁對立說（『或謂太初為「無」』——「有」豈能生於「無」？），繼而：『有』意念『願我為多、願我生長』，遂生出火；火生水；水生食。萬物由諸元素依比例合成（『十六分』之說），『有』入於每一物、每物以其內之活我為心，成為多者之名與形——每一自我中的自我。結尾之頌驚人：『汝是女、汝是男、汝是少年與少女……汝是扶杖老人；汝向一切方位而生。』譬喻為此章之妙，逐一消解部分與整體之界：一團泥土——知其一團即知一切泥製品，『變化僅是言語、是名』；蜂之蜜——採百花而成一體，精粹無以分辨；諸河——奔流入海即成海，海『不知此是那條河』；榕樹籽——剖開無樹——『彼微妙者乃萬有之自我』；鹽——溶於水不可見而每一口皆嘗得，自面至底——『汝於此身不見「有」，然「有」實在此處：汝即彼』。功能：此為「有」（sat）作為宇宙唯一實體、個體與絕對同一不二之教；tat tvam asi 成為吠檀多四大『偈』之一；師徒問答之框架——固執而誠摯的學生、自泥土升至鹽的意象——成為後世一切傳法場景的範本；對「無」的反駁標誌傳統內部「有」與「無」創世觀最古老的存世辯論，與無有歌的開放疑問相呼應。

functions: Foundational doctrine of sat (Being) as the one substance of the cosmos
Model of guru-to-student pedagogy through escalating parables
Mahavakya 'tat tvam asi' - charter of Vedantic identity of self and absolute
Oldest surviving in-tradition debate against non-being (asat) cosmogony

variants.name: Nasadiya Sukta's open doubt
variants.summary: The Vedic hymn poses creation as unknowable - no one knows whether a maker made it; the Chandogya answers with confident pedagogy, while keeping the 'one only, without a second' refrain.

variants.name: Brihadaranyaka's Self-alone creation
variants.summary: The personified sibling: the Self alone, fearing and desiring, divides itself; Chandogya de-personalizes the same monism into Being and its manifestations.

variants.name: Shankara's commentary (Vedanta)
variants.summary: The non-dualist reading that fixed the chapter's authority: 'Being' is Brahman, the parables a graded approach to nonduality, and 'that thou art' taken as literal identity.

title.zh: 摩根德耶見劫滅之異象

region.zh: 尼彌沙林中仙居（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Markandeya-Samasya), composition layers c. 400 BCE-400 CE (Ganguli translation, 1883-96)

source.work: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, trans. K. M. Ganguli (1883-96), Vana Parva, Markandeya's deluge vision (the child on the banyan leaf)

summary.en: In the forest, the aged seer Markandeya - the only being to survive every dissolution - answers Yudhishthira's questions about the end of the world: drought burns the earth, fires consume it, the oceans drink the world dry, and then the Lord sleeps alone on the waters. In the vision's heart, Markandeya sees himself drawn inside the sleeping child's body and finds the whole universe there, intact, with himself living within it.
summary.zh: 林中，經歷一切劫滅而獨存的年邁仙人摩根德耶回答堅戰關於世界終結的提問：大旱焚地、大火毀世、海洋飲盡世界，其後主獨臥於水上。異象核心處，摩根德耶被吸入沉睡孩童之身，竟於其中見完整宇宙，而他自己亦在其中生活。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition (epic recitation, temple discourse). Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: Yudhishthira, grieving and unsettled after years of forest exile, asks the old seer Markandeya to tell him what happens when the age ends. Markandeya, ancient beyond all others, answers that he alone has seen it: he has lived through a thousand dissolutions, and each time only he and the Lord remain. When the age runs out, a twelve-year drought sears the earth; creatures weaken and die; then the seven suns blaze, and fire consumes the three worlds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Markandeya-Samasya sections (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: The world burns like a cauldron's rim in the fire; the mountains tumble; the ocean, swollen, drinks the earth and then is itself swallowed, drawn up into a sky gone dark; darkness covers everything, and in that undivided night the wind alone moves. Then the Lord, Narayana, lies down upon the waters, alone, the sole being in the universes' sleep - the cosmos that was is wound up in him like a bed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Markandeya-Samasya sections (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the midst of that expanse Markandeya sees a banyan tree, and on a single leaf a small child, dark and lovely, asleep, sucking its toe. Drawn by an inexplicable tenderness, the sage approaches; the child smiles, opens its mouth, breathes him in - and Markandeya finds himself inside a world: oceans, mountains, cities, kingdoms, his own hermitage, people who know him, a life going on. He wanders this interior universe for years, seeking its edge, until at last the child breathes him out again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Markandeya-Samasya sections (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

passages.text: Waking outside, the sage understands: the child is the Lord of all; the world is held inside him as a dream in a sleeper, creation his breathing out and dissolution his breathing in. The child smiles, identifies himself as the beginning, middle and end of all, and departs into the waters. Markandeya returns to the Pandavas with the certainty that only Vishnu stands when all else falls, and that the world's catastrophes are the motions of his sleep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Markandeya-Samasya sections (Ganguli 1883-96); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Kisari Mohan Ganguli, The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, 1883-96 (public domain); modern: J. A. B. van Buitenen, The Mahabharata, vol. 3 (Vana Parva, incomplete), University of Chicago Press, 1975

narrative.en:
The Markandeya-Samasya section of the Vana Parva is the Mahabharata's principal eschatology: during the Pandavas' forest exile, the brothers come to the hermitage of the impossibly old seer Markandeya, and Yudhishthira - still reeling from his losses - asks the questions a bereaved king asks a survivor of everything: how does the world end, what remains, who rules after?

Markandeya's credentials frame the answer: he alone has lived through prior dissolutions, the sole being besides the Lord to remain when each kalpa closes. His account of the end is a sequence of un-creations. First, a twelve-year drought scorches the earth, and living things weaken as in a great famine. Then the seven suns rise and blaze; fire seizes the three worlds, and the world burns 'like the rim of a cauldron' - mountains topple, the sky itself smokes. The ocean, swollen with the melting world, first drinks the earth, then is swallowed in turn, drawn up as vapor into a sky gone dark. Nothing differentiates; darkness is undivided; only the wind still moves in the void. And in that night, the Lord - Narayana-Vishnu - lies down alone on the waters: the cosmos that was is wound up in him 'like a bed being rolled away', and he sleeps, the single being in the universes' rest.

The vision at the center is the epic's most famous image of interiority. In the featureless waters Markandeya sees a banyan tree; on one of its leaves, a small child - dark, lovely, asleep, sucking its toe. The old sage approaches with inexplicable tenderness, and the child smiles and opens its mouth. Markandeya is breathed in - and finds himself inside a complete world: seas and mountains, cities and rivers, his own hermitage, people who greet him by name, a whole life going on. He wanders this interior universe for what feels like years, searching for its edge, unable to find it; the inhabitants know nothing of being inside anyone. At last the child exhales, and the sage stands again on the leaf's rim, outside, looking at the sleeper.

The child wakes, smiles, and identifies himself: he is the beginning, the middle, and the end; the worlds are held in him as dreams are held by a sleeper; creation is his breathing out, dissolution his breathing in. (The episode thus fuses the epic's flood-with-Vishnu imagery with an almost Buddhist dream-ontology.) The child then departs into the waters, and Markandeya returns to the Pandavas with his doctrine: only Vishnu stands when everything falls; the catastrophes of worlds are the motions of his sleep; and the wise, knowing this, hold to dharma in the meantime - for the age will end, but the Self who witnesses it will not.

Function: this is the mythological engine of Hindu cyclical time - the same imagery the Vishnu Purana systematizes into kalpas, manvantaras and pralayas - and the epic's consolation for exile and loss: the world's destruction is real but contained; the container sleeps gently. The child-on-the-leaf image becomes the icon of Bhagavata devotion centuries later (Vishnu as the infant on the banyan leaf), and Markandeya becomes the tradition's recurring witness - the one who remembers, because he survives.
narrative.zh: 大森林篇之摩根德耶章為摩訶婆羅多主要末世論：般度五子在林居期間造訪年邁逾古的仙人摩根德耶之居所，堅戰仍為其失所動搖，向這位經歷一切而倖存者提出亡國之君的問題：世界如何終結？終結之後何者存留？摩根德耶的資歷框定答案：唯有他經歷過先前的劫滅，每一劫閉合之時，除主之外唯他獨存。他對終結的描述是一連串『逆創世』：先是十二年大旱灼燒大地，眾生如逢大饑而衰；繼而七日並出，烈火抓住三界，世界『如鍋沿』般燃燒——群山傾倒，天穹自亦冒煙。海因融化的世界而漲，先飲大地，繼而被吞，化為水汽升入昏暗之天。萬象無別，黑暗不分，唯風仍行於虛空。彼夜，主——那羅延-毘濕奴——獨臥於水上：曾為宇宙之物在彼之中『如床被捲起』般收攏，彼獨眠，為諸宇宙之息中唯一存者。中央的異象是史詩最著名的內在性意象：在無別之水上，摩根德耶見一株榕樹；一片葉上有一小童——膚色深美，熟睡，吮著腳趾。老仙人懷著無以名狀的慈愛走近；孩童微笑張口。摩根德耶被吸入——竟發現自己身在一個完整的世界：海洋群山、城池河流、他自己的仙居、以名相稱的人們，一整個生活正在進行。他漫遊這內在宇宙數年之久，尋覓其邊界而不可得；居民無人知道自己身處他人之內。最後孩童呼氣，仙人復立於葉緣之外，注視沉睡者。孩童醒來微笑，自陳：彼是始、中、終；諸世界如夢被睡者所持；創世是其呼氣，劫滅是其吸氣。（此幕遂將史詩的毘濕奴洪水意象與近乎佛教的夢之存在論熔於一爐。）孩童沒入水中，摩根德耶攜其教義歸告般度諸子：萬物傾覆之時唯毘濕奴獨立；世界之災乃其睡眠之動；智者知此，於其間持守正法——劫數將至，而見證之自我不滅。功能：此為印度循環時間觀之神話引擎（毘濕奴往世書將同一意象系統化為劫、摩奴期與滅劫），亦是史詩對流放與喪失的慰藉——世界之毀滅真實而受容；容納者溫柔地睡著。『葉上孩童』之像於數世紀後成為奉愛的圖像（毘濕奴為榕葉上的嬰兒），摩根德耶亦成為傳統中反覆現身的見證者——因他倖存，故他記得。

title.en: The Four Ages and the Three Dissolutions (Vishnu Purana)
title.zh: 四期與三滅劫（毘濕奴往世書）

summary.en: The Purana turns cosmic vision into arithmetic: the four ages (Krita, Treta, Dvapara, Kali) tick down like a clock losing its feet; each kalpa of a thousand ages is Brahma's day, each night a dissolution; and when Brahma's own life ends, the elements themselves dissolve into the Lord. Three kinds of pralaya are distinguished - and only the third is final, and only for a single soul.
summary.zh: 往世書將宇宙異象化為算術：四期（圓滿、三分、二分、爭鬥）如失足之鐘般倒數；千期為梵天一日，一夜即一滅劫；梵天自身壽盡時，諸元素亦溶解於主。滅劫分三種——唯第三種是終極，且僅對單一靈魂而言。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition (recited in temple discourse and scholarly study). Classified 'myth' (Puranic cosmological narrative).

passages.text: The ages are four: the Krita (perfect), the Treta, the Dvapara and the Kali. In the first, dharma stands on all four of its feet and men live long, equal and joyful; in each following age, dharma loses one foot, men's stature and years diminish, and virtue decays by quarters. The ages have dawns and twilights as well as middles, and the whole four, measured in divine years, amount to twelve thousand.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, ch. 3 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

passages.text: A thousand of such four-age cycles is a day of Brahma, and his night is of equal length. At day's end, when the night of Brahma falls, creation is dissolved: the three worlds, consumed, are withdrawn into the waters, and the Lord abides upon the serpent's coil, holding the seed of the world as fire holds its heat and the seed its sprout - dormant, but not destroyed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, ch. 3 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

passages.text: Three dissolutions are taught. The occasional (naimittika) is the night of Brahma: creatures and worlds are withdrawn, and arise again at dawn. The elemental (prakritika) comes when Brahma's own life runs out: earth dissolves into water, water into fire, fire into air, air into ether, until only the Lord and primitive matter remain. The absolute (atyantika) is individual: the liberation of a soul, which ends for it all future dissolution. After Brahma's death the next Brahma wakes, and the wheel turns again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Vishnu Purana, Book 1, chs. 3, 6 (Wilson 1840); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Horace Hayman Wilson, The Vishnu Purana: A System of Hindu Mythology and Tradition, London, 1840 (public domain); modern survey: Ludo Rocher, The Puranas, Wiesbaden, 1986

narrative.en:
The Vishnu Purana's opening books convert the epic's apocalyptic visions (Markandeya's, Krishna's at Kurukshetra) into a complete cosmological timetable - the architecture of Hindu time that everything from temple festivals to astrological almanacs assumes.

The ages: time is a four-beat cycle. In the Krita (or Satya) age, dharma stands on all four feet; human beings live for centuries, equal in fortune and virtue, and no one needs to labor for truth - it is simply present. In the Treta, one foot is lost; in the Dvapara, two; in the Kali, dharma stands on one foot alone, and the age's signature is mixture - kingship by wealth, holiness by costume, truth bought and sold, bodies shorter and lives briefer. The ages run on a declining staircase, each shorter than the last, with dawns and twilights (sandhyas) at their edges; the four together, counted in divine years, make twelve thousand divine years - and a divine year is three hundred and sixty mortal ones. We live, says the Purana, deep in the Kali.

The calendar of worlds: a thousand of these four-age cycles is one day of Brahma, a kalpa; Brahma's night is equal. At each nightfall comes the first dissolution - the occasional or naimittika: the three worlds are consumed and withdrawn into the waters, and Brahma-Vishnu sleeps on the coils of the world-serpent Shesha, holding the world-seed 'as fire holds its heat, as the seed holds the sprout' - dormant, not dead. At dawn the creation resumes exactly where the timetable left off; the accumulated past is not erased but archived in the sleeper.

The second dissolution - elemental or prakritika - is vaster: when Brahma's own life completes its hundred years (each of his years a thousand kalpas), not only creatures but the elements themselves are rolled up: earth dissolves into water, water into fire, fire into air, air into ether, ether into its unmanifest source, until nothing remains but the Lord and primal matter (prakriti) in their embrace. Then - there is no dramatic 'then'; the Purana is content with the wheel - a new Brahma wakes and the kalpas begin again. The third dissolution is not cosmic at all: the atyantika ('absolute') dissolution is the individual soul's liberation - the one exit from the wheel, available to any being at any time, which ends for that soul all future endings.

Function: this arithmetic did three things to the tradition. It made every temple festival a punctual event on a cosmic clock (the almanacs locate us in the 28th four-age cycle of the 7th manvantara of Brahma's 51st year); it turned moral decline into a cosmology - the Kali age's corruption is built into the structure of time, so history has a direction without a final end; and it gave the renouncer a third option no apocalypse offers: to exit time entirely rather than wait for its renewal. Compared with Ragnarok or Revelation, the Hindu pralaya is neither final nor tragic - it is a breath held between syllables of an endless recitation.
narrative.zh: 毘濕奴往世書開篇將史詩的末世異象（摩根德耶、克里希那於俱盧之野）轉化為完整的宇宙時間表——從寺廟節慶到占星曆書所預設的印度時間架構。諸期：時間為四拍循環。圓滿期（Krita/Satya），正法四足而立；人壽數百年，福報德行均等，真理不假外求。三分期失一足；二分期失二足；至爭鬥期（Kali），正法僅餘一足，其時代的印記是混雜——以財富立王權、以服飾立聖潔、真理可買賣，身短壽促。諸期沿下行階梯遞短，邊緣有晨昏（sandhyas）；四期合計以神年計一萬二千神年——一神年為三百六十人年。往世書言：吾人現處爭鬥期之深處。世界曆法：一千個四期循環為梵天之一日（一劫 kalpa）；梵天之夜等長。每次夜臨便是第一種滅劫——間滅（naimittika）：三界被消耗並收攝入水，梵天-毘濕奴眠於世界蛇謝沙之盤曲上，持世界之種『如火持其熱、如種持其芽』——蟄伏而非死亡。黎明時創世依時表續行，累積的過去不被抹去，而被封存於睡眠者之中。第二種滅劫——元滅（prakritika）——更為浩大：當梵天自身壽命圓滿其百年（彼之一年等於一千劫），不只眾生，連元素本身亦被捲起：地溶於水、水溶於火、火溶於風、風溶於空，空溶於其不顯之源，直至唯餘主與原初質料（prakriti）相擁。然後——並無戲劇性的『然後』，往世書安於車輪——新梵天醒來，諸劫再始。第三種滅劫全然非宇宙性：終滅（atyantika）乃個體靈魂之解脫——唯一離開車輪的出口，任何時刻任何眾生皆可得，從此終結其一切未來的終結。功能：此算術為傳統做了三件事——使每場廟會成為宇宙時鐘上的準點事件；將道德衰退化為宇宙論——爭鬥期的腐化內建於時間結構，歷史因有方向而無終點；並給予出離者一個任何末日論皆不提供的第三選項：徹底離開時間，而非等待其更新。與諸神黃昏或啟示錄相比，印度滅劫既非終極亦非悲劇——它是無盡誦念的音節之間的一次屏息。

functions: Architecture of Hindu cyclical time (yugas, kalpas, manvantaras) used by calendars and ritual
Cosmologization of moral decline: the Kali age built into time's structure
Doctrine of three dissolutions - periodic, elemental, and individual (liberation)
Devotional and philosophical contrast-case to linear apocalypse traditions

summary.en: Washing at morning in the river, Manu finds a tiny fish in his joined hands. The fish begs to be reared - 'rear me, I will save thee' - and grows through jar, trough, pit and ocean until it is mountain-sized. When the deluge comes, Manu builds the ship, ties its rope to the fish's horn, and is towed through the drowning world to the northern mountain. From his sacrifice, and the waters' deposit, a woman arises: 'in her the race was born.'
summary.zh: 清晨於河中沐浴時，摩奴合掌得一小魚。魚懇求飼養——『養我，我將救你』——經罐、槽、坑、海而成山岳般巨獸。洪水來時，摩奴造舟，以繩繫於魚角，被拖曳過滅世之水，抵北方之山。由其祭祀與水中沉積，一位女子生於其間：『族類由她而生。』

sensitivity.note: Living tradition: Manu is the named progenitor in ritual law and the flood story is retold in Matsya imagery. Classified 'myth'.

passages.text: There was a rishi called Manu, son of Vivasvat, famed in austerity. One morning, bringing water for the oblation in his joined hands, he found a small fish in his palms. The fish spoke: 'Rear me, I will save thee.' Manu asked where it came from; the fish answered only that it was in his hands - nourish it, for a flood would carry off all creatures, and it would save him from the flood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shatapatha Brahmana 1.8.1 (Eggeling 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The fish asked in what vessel it should be reared. Manu said 'in a jar'; the fish outgrew the jar and asked for a trough, outgrew the trough and asked for a large pit, outgrew the pit and asked for the ocean - Manu carried it to the sea. The fish then told him the year of the flood and the means: 'Build a ship; bring in it the seven seers; stow the seeds of all things, pair by pair; and when the waters rise, fasten the ship to me - I will have a horn, and thou shalt tie the rope to it.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shatapatha Brahmana 1.8.1 (Eggeling 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: And in that same year, as the fish had foretold, Manu built the ship, paid homage to the fish, and loaded it with the seeds. The flood arose and swept away all creatures; Manu alone was left, in his ship tethered to the fish's horn. The fish swam - across the drowned earth, through waters rolling like the sea - northward to the northern mountain, and said: 'I have saved thee. Fasten the ship to this tree; descend thou gently, slowly, as the water subsides.' Manu descended - and therefore the northern slope is called 'the descent of Manu'.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shatapatha Brahmana 1.8.1 (Eggeling 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The flood had carried off every living being; Manu alone was left. Desiring offspring, he sacrificed diligently: butter, milk, whey and curds he offered in the waters. In the first year a woman arose from them, wet, ointment trickling from her; Mitra and Varuna passed by and claimed her, but she went to Manu. 'From the very seed thou hast begotten in the waters,' she said, 'thou hast placed me in the waters. Make me thy mate; in me the race shall be born.' Manu was unwilling at first; they sacrificed together - and 'in her, this race was born': she is Ida, the mother of this offspring.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Shatapatha Brahmana 1.8.1 (Eggeling 1882); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Julius Eggeling, The Satapatha-Brahmana, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 12), Oxford, 1882 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The flood of Manu - in the Shatapatha Brahmana, the oldest continuous telling of the deluge in Indian literature - is the Vedic ritual corpus' own Noah story, told inside a manual of sacrifice to explain a rite: why morning oblations begin with water held in the joined hands.

The beginning is almost domestic. Manu, son of Vivasvat (the Sun), a seer 'famed in austerity', brings water for his morning oblation with cupped hands, and finds in his palms a small fish that speaks. 'Rear me, I will save thee' - the fish does not explain at first, only repeats that a flood will carry off all creatures. Manu, courteously incredulous, asks what will become of it; the fish's answer escalates with its body. Reared in a jar, it outgrows the jar; moved to a trough, it outgrows the trough; a large pit suffices briefly; then the sea. Manu carries it - the story's quiet comedy is that the future savior of the world must be carried in ever-larger household vessels - and the fish, grown vast, gives the logistics: in such-and-such a year the flood will come; build a ship; load the seven seers; stow the seeds of all things, pair by pair; when the water rises, tie the ship's rope to the horn I will have grown.

The flood comes 'in that same year'. It is total: 'the flood swept away all creatures; Manu alone was left'. The fish tows the tethered ship through rivers, across the drowned earth, northward to the northern mountain - where it tells Manu he is saved, to fasten the ship to a tree, and to descend slowly as the water falls. (The Brahmana adds the aition: the mountain's northern slope is called 'Manu's descent' - the landscape remembers.)

The rebeginning is the strangest part. The flood has left Manu alone and - the text is careful - desiring offspring. He sacrifices: butter, milk, whey, curds, offered into the waters. In the first year, from the sacrifice, a woman arises, dripping; the gods Mitra and Varuna pass by and claim her for themselves, but she comes to Manu. Asked for whom she was born, she answers that she is made from the very seed Manu poured into the waters - his sacrifice made flesh. 'Make me thy mate; in me the race shall be born.' After a joint sacrifice, they unite, and the Brahmana concludes: 'in her this race was born' - she is Ida, mother of humanity.

Function and lineage: the story does double duty as flood myth and sacrifice charter - the deluge is survived by ritual, and the new humanity is generated by an offering rather than by the survivor's children alone. The Puranic versions expand it into the Matsya avatar: Vishnu himself is the fish, warning Manu (Vaivasvata) and preserving the Vedas as well as the seeds; the Mahabharata retells it in the Markandeya section; the iconography is the temple panel of Vishnu-fish towing the boat. In the cross-tradition flood cluster, this is the Vedic-Hindu anchor: survival by animal guide, rescue of the seeds of life, landing on a mountain - with the distinctive Hindu signature that the rescuer is the god who will be worshipped forever after, and that a sacrifice, not a family, restarts the world.
narrative.zh: 摩奴洪水——見於薩塔帕塔梵書，印度文獻中最古老的連貫洪水敘事——是吠陀祭祀文獻自身的『挪亞』故事，嵌於祭祀手冊之中，用以解釋一項儀式：為何晨祭以合掌捧水開始。開端近乎家常。摩奴，毗首竭之子（日神之子），『以苦行聞名』的仙人，清晨合掌捧祭水，於掌中得一小魚，魚能言語：『養我，我將救你』——魚起初不作解釋，只重申洪水將席捲一切眾生。摩奴禮貌地半信半疑，問其何往；魚的回答隨其身軀而升級：養於罐中，罐不足以容；移於槽，槽不足；掘大坑，坑不足；直至入海。摩奴以越來越大的家用器皿搬運這位未來的世界救主——神話的靜默喜劇——而後長成的魚交付後勤細節：某年洪水將至；造舟；載七仙人；貯藏萬物之種，一對一對；水漲時，以繩繫舟於我所生之角。洪水『於同年』而至，且是全然的：『洪水捲走一切眾生；唯摩奴存焉。』魚拖曳繫舟渡河、越滅世大地、北行至北方之山——在那裡告訴摩奴：你得救了；把船繫於樹；水退時緩緩下行。（梵書補充詞源：山之北坡名『摩奴降處』——地貌記得。）重生之部分最奇特：洪水後摩奴獨存且——經文審慎地說——渴望後嗣。他祭祀：酥油、乳、乳清、凝乳，祭入水中。第一年，自祭中生一女子，滴著水；密多羅與伐樓那經過欲納之，她卻走向摩奴。問她為誰而生，她答：由你親自祭入水中的種子所造——你的祭祀成為肉身。『使我為伴；族類將由我而生。』二人合祭之後結合，梵書結語：『族類由她而生』——她即伊陀，人類之母。功能與譜系：故事兼任洪水神話與祭祀憲章——倖存於洪水者靠儀式，新人類由祭品而非倖存者之子女獨自生成。往世書版本擴充為摩蹉化身：毘濕奴親為魚，警示摩奴（婆藪瓦陀），並保存吠陀與萬物之種；摩訶婆羅多於摩根德耶章重述；廟宇浮雕為拖舟的毘濕奴魚。在跨傳統洪水母題群中，此為吠陀-印度之錨：動物嚮導之救、生命之種之存、泊於山巔——帶著鮮明的印度印記：救者正是其後永受崇拜之神，且重啟世界的是一場祭祀，而非一個家族。

functions: Flood myth of the Indian tradition - survival by divine fish, seeds of life, mountain landing
Charter of morning water-oblations (the cupped-hands rite re-enacts Manu's finding)
Foundation of human descent from Manu, progenitor named in later law and ritual
Matrix of the Matsya avatar (Puranic expansion) and temple iconography

variants.name: Matsya avatar version (Vishnu Purana; Bhagavata 8.24)
variants.summary: The fish is Vishnu's first avatar, and the cargo expands: the Vedas (stolen and hidden by a demon) are recovered as well as the seeds; Manu Vaivasvata is a king - deluge, scripture-rescue and incarnation fused.

variants.name: Mahabharata retelling (Markandeya section)
variants.summary: The epic retells the Brahmana story with Markandeya as witness, aligning the historical flood with the cosmic dissolution and adding Manu's descendants as the lineage of kings.

variants.name: Utnapishtim's flood (Gilgamesh XI)
variants.summary: The closest Mesopotamian parallel: divine warning, a vessel with the seed of life, an animal guide, mountain landing, and a post-flood rite - the shared ancient flood grammar.

variants.name: Noah's flood (Genesis 6-9)
variants.summary: Parallel cluster member: divine warning, vessel with animal pairs, mountain landing, covenant rite - with the moral-theological frame of human wickedness and a binding covenant.

texts.sensitivity_guidance: The story is retold in living religious education and Matsya imagery remains in temple art; quote public-domain translations; note which version (Brahmana vs Purana avatar) is meant, as they differ on who the fish is.
